blocks.text: **The problem.** Given an integer array `nums`, return the number of **reverse pairs**: index pairs `i < j` with `nums[i] > 2 · nums[j]`.

blocks.alt: Counting across two sorted halves, 1, 2, 3 and 1, 3. For the left value 3, the right values smaller than 3 divided by 2 — just 1 — count: one pair. For 1 and 2 nothing counts. Because both halves are sorted, the pointer into the right half only moves forward as the left value grows.

nums = [1, 3, 2, 3, 1]  ->  2   (3 > 2·1 at indexes 1,4 and 3,4)
nums = [2, 4, 3, 5, 1]  ->  3   (4, 3 and 5 are each more than 2·1)

blocks.text: The idea: count across sorted halves with two pointers

It's Count Inversions with a different condition. Split in half; pairs inside each half are counted recursively; pairs **across** the halves are counted while both halves are sorted. But the condition `a[i] > 2 · a[j]` doesn't match the merge's own comparison, so do a **separate counting pass** first: for each left value `a[i]` in increasing order, move `j` forward through the right half while `a[i] > 2 · a[j]`. Since `a[i]` only grows, `j` never moves back — the whole pass is linear. Then merge as usual.
**Time O(n²), space O(1).** Too slow for 5 × 10⁴ values.
2. Merge sort with a counting pass

blocks.caption: Before each merge, two pointers count the pairs across the sorted halves in one sweep.

blocks.code:
def reverse_pairs(nums):
    a = list(nums)

    def sort_count(lo, hi):               # sorts a[lo:hi], returns the reverse pairs inside it
        if hi - lo <= 1:
            return 0
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        count = sort_count(lo, mid) + sort_count(mid, hi)
        j = mid
        for i in range(lo, mid):          # both halves are sorted: j only moves forward
            while j < hi and a[i] > 2 * a[j]:
                j += 1
            count += j - mid              # a[mid:j] are all small enough for a[i]
        a[lo:hi] = sorted(a[lo:hi])       # merge (sorted() on two sorted runs is linear in Timsort)
        return count

    return sort_count(0, len(a))

blocks.text: **Time O(n log n), space O(n).** Each level does one linear counting pass and one linear merge. In Java and C++, compute `2 * a[j]` in 64 bits — with values up to 2³¹ − 1 it overflows an int.

blocks.alt: Every pair: O(n²) time, O(1) space. Merge sort + counting pass: O(n log n) time, O(n) space.

blocks.text: A Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) over the compressed values solves it in O(n log n) too — useful when the condition can't be counted with two pointers.

items: **Counting inside the merge loop** — the merge's comparison is `a[p] <= a[q]`, not the pair condition; keep the passes separate.
**Count Inversions** — the condition `a[i] > a[j]` fits inside the merge itself. Previous lesson.
**Count of Range Sum** — merge sort on prefix sums, counting pairs whose difference falls in a range.
**Count of Smaller Numbers After Self** — per-index counts through the same merge.
